The Lighthouse Keeper's Ledger

Every evening at a quarter past six, Mara climbed the ninety-one steps to the lamp room and wrote one line in the ledger. The line was never about the weather, although the weather was the only thing that ever changed. It was about what she had noticed. On Monday she noticed that the gulls had stopped landing on the north rail. On Tuesday she noticed that the sea had the colour of old pewter, and that the fishing boats came home early.

The ledger had belonged to her grandfather, and before him to a man whose name had been rubbed off the cover by a century of salt. Mara did not know what the earlier keepers had noticed. The first forty pages were missing! Someone had torn them out, carefully, close to the spine, and she had spent a long winter wondering why.

"You could ask the harbour master," her brother said when he visited in spring. "He keeps everything."

"He keeps receipts," Mara answered. "This is not a receipt."

She was wrong about that, as it turned out. In June a parcel arrived from the mainland, wrapped in brown paper and tied with the kind of string nobody used any more. Inside were the forty pages. Each one carried a single line, in a hand that leaned to the left, and each line began with the same three words: I did not. I did not light the lamp on the night of the storm. I did not answer the bell. I did not tell them about the boat.

Mara read the pages twice, then she climbed the ninety-one steps and lit the lamp a full hour early. The beam swung out over the pewter water; the gulls, for reasons of their own, returned to the north rail. She opened the ledger to a fresh page and wrote: I did. Then she wrote the date, which was a Thursday, and underlined it twice.

Nothing happened that night, or the night after. But the fishing boats began to stay out later, and the harbour master sent a second parcel, which contained nothing but a key. Mara hung the key on a nail beside the door. She did not know what it opened. She noticed it every evening, at a quarter past six, and that seemed to be enough.

Years later, when the lamp was automated and the stairs were closed to the public, a volunteer found the ledger in a drawer. The last entry was dated in a steady hand. It read: the sea is the colour of pewter again, and I have finally stopped counting the steps.
